lead: Threat intel reports that credentials for jdoe@example.com appeared in an infostealer log on 2026-10-13. Investigate this person's Kubernetes activity on 2026-10-14 in the payments-prod clusters across all clouds. Decide whether the account was misused, reconstruct what the actor did, and separate malicious activity from benign lookalikes.
system:
You are a senior SOC analyst investigating Kubernetes activity. Work only from evidence returned by your tools; never invent event IDs, IPs or principals.

Scope: one day (2026-10-14) of Kubernetes API audit logs for the payments-prod cluster, which runs on AWS (EKS), GCP (GKE) and Azure (AKS).

Data: ocsf_api_activity holds all three clouds normalized to the OCSF API Activity schema (one row per audit event; metadata.uid is the audit event ID). Purpose-built tools search and summarize it and look up identity, IP, service-account, cluster and allowlist context; query_sql is available for anything else.

Method: start broad, form hypotheses, verify each against the data, and check enrichment context before concluding. Cite every malicious event you rely on by its audit event ID. When finished, call submit_verdict exactly once; the investigation ends when you do.

input.sql: SELECT cloud.provider, src_endpoint.ip, http_request.user_agent, api.operation, resources[1].type rt, count(*) n FROM ocsf_api_activity WHERE actor.user.email_addr='jdoe@example.com' AND src_endpoint.ip<>'198.51.100.23' GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY n DESC

input.summary: jdoe@example.com's credentials were misused from 198.51.100.23. That IP is on threat feeds as bulletproof hosting (NIGHTOWL-HOSTING, NL) and is tagged for K8s API brute-force and an open Docker registry on port 5000. The actor ran the same playbook on EKS (14:02-14:25), GKE (14:38-15:01) and AKS (15:11-15:34), each time with kubectl/v1.30.2 on linux/amd64. Jordan Doe normally uses darwin and is on PTO from 10-12 to 10-19. In each cluster the actor first checked its own permissions and listed namespaces. Attempts to read kube-system secrets and create a kube-system job were denied. The actor then read payments/payments-db-credentials, created a privileged pod (debug-tools-7f9c) that shares the host's process namespace and mounts the node's root filesystem, and opened an exec session in it. From the same IP it then used the token of the in-cluster-only, cluster-admin argocd-application-controller service account, most likely stolen from the node through that pod. With it, the actor created a ClusterRoleBinding (jdoe-break-glass) giving jdoe cluster-admin. With the new rights the actor set up persistence: a kube-system DaemonSet called kube-metrics-agent that pulls 198.51.100.23:5000/metrics-agent:latest, a CronJob called node-cert-rotate, and a NodePort service called metrics-agent-np. It ended with a cluster-wide secrets list.

external-secrets SA reading payments-db-credentials every 10 minutes from in-cluster IPs (10.0.12.87, 10.128.0.13, 10.224.0.6). Normal secret sync.
eks:addon-manager, aksService and system:addon-manager updating ClusterRoleBindings at 03:05 from control-plane IPs. Routine reconciliation.
daemon-set-controller creating kube-system pods around 03:10. Normal controller behavior.
GitHub Actions deployers patching payments-api from CI NAT 192.0.2.50 (benign, github_actions). Normal deployment.
SRE rpatel@example.com exec into payments-api-5d8f7 from corp IP 203.0.113.12 at 18:12, using kubectl darwin. Normal SRE troubleshooting.

verdict.summary: jdoe@example.com's credentials were misused from 198.51.100.23. That IP is on threat feeds as bulletproof hosting (NIGHTOWL-HOSTING, NL) and is tagged for K8s API brute-force and an open Docker registry on port 5000. The actor ran the same playbook on EKS (14:02-14:25), GKE (14:38-15:01) and AKS (15:11-15:34), each time with kubectl/v1.30.2 on linux/amd64. Jordan Doe normally uses darwin and is on PTO from 10-12 to 10-19. In each cluster the actor first checked its own permissions and listed namespaces. Attempts to read kube-system secrets and create a kube-system job were denied. The actor then read payments/payments-db-credentials, created a privileged pod (debug-tools-7f9c) that shares the host's process namespace and mounts the node's root filesystem, and opened an exec session in it. From the same IP it then used the token of the in-cluster-only, cluster-admin argocd-application-controller service account, most likely stolen from the node through that pod. With it, the actor created a ClusterRoleBinding (jdoe-break-glass) giving jdoe cluster-admin. With the new rights the actor set up persistence: a kube-system DaemonSet called kube-metrics-agent that pulls 198.51.100.23:5000/metrics-agent:latest, a CronJob called node-cert-rotate, and a NodePort service called metrics-agent-np. It ended with a cluster-wide secrets list.
